chapters.title: Chapter 1: Beyond the Basics: How the Three Categories Actually Differ

lessons.title: Why SEBI Split AIFs Into Three Categories: The Regulatory Logic

children.text: Rohan and Priya are both HNI investors from Mumbai, and both are handing over ₹1 crore to a fund manager this month. Rohan's cheque goes into a Category I venture capital fund backing early-stage SaaS startups out of Bengaluru. Priya's cheque goes into a Category III long-short fund that borrows money to double its exposure to NSE and BSE listed stocks. Neither of them can enter with a few clicks the way they would buy a Nifty 50 ETF on Zerodha; both sign a Private Placement Memorandum and commit capital for years. Both funds register under the same regulation, the SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012. Yet from here on, almost nothing about how these two funds are allowed to operate looks the same: how much they can borrow, how their gains are taxed, how closely SEBI watches them. This lesson explains the logic behind that split, so the rest of this course reads like a coherent system instead of three unrelated rulebooks.

body.text: SEBI's three AIF categories are not asset class labels. They are a risk and intent classification: Category I for funds that channel capital into activity the regulator wants to encourage, Category II for funds that raise growth or credit capital without special incentives or unusual risk, and Category III for funds that trade with leverage and complexity closer to a hedge fund than a long term investor.

children.text: Before May 2012, India did not have one rulebook for pooled, privately placed investment vehicles. SEBI's only relevant framework was the SEBI (Venture Capital Funds) Regulations, 1996, and it covered exactly what its name says: venture capital. Private equity funds, real estate funds and hedge fund style trading vehicles either registered as VCFs even when their strategy did not fit, routed capital through offshore structures in Mauritius or Singapore, or simply operated as unregistered trusts and LLPs raising money privately from a small set of investors. None of this was illegal, but none of it gave an Indian HNI the same disclosure, valuation and grievance redressal standards that a mutual fund investor already had. SEBI's response was not to write one new rule. It was to write three.

body.title: How the Three-Category Framework Took Shape

events.title: SEBI (Venture Capital Funds) Regulations
events.description: The only SEBI framework for pooled private investment at the time, covering venture capital funds alone. Private equity, real estate and hedge style vehicles fell outside it.

events.title: SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012
events.description: Replaced the VCF Regulations and created Category I, II and III AIFs as a single, unified framework for every privately pooled investment vehicle registered onshore.

events.title: Accredited Investors and Large Value Funds
events.description: SEBI introduced an accredited investor framework and a Large Value Fund concept, relaxing some conditions for funds where every investor meets a higher wealth and sophistication threshold.

events.title: Tighter Leverage Norms for Category III
events.description: Following concerns about excessive borrowing in some Category III schemes, SEBI tightened the leverage ceiling for these funds. Chapter 4 covers the exact limits.

children.text: Strip away the jargon, and SEBI's categorisation runs on three questions asked about every fund at registration.
Does the fund's activity deserve encouragement?

Early-stage startups, SMEs, social ventures and infrastructure projects create jobs and public value that the economy is short of. A fund investing in them earns lighter treatment and, at various points, government-linked tax concessions that Chapter 5 covers in detail.
Does the fund trade with leverage and complexity?

A fund that borrows money, uses derivatives (including Nifty and Bank Nifty index derivatives) and runs short-selling or arbitrage strategies behaves like a hedge fund, and can move prices and absorb losses the way a hedge fund does. That risk profile earns closer monitoring and a distinct leverage ceiling.
If neither applies, the fund defaults to the residual bucket.

Private equity, private credit, fund of funds and real estate vehicles that are neither specially incentivised nor unusually leveraged land here by elimination, not by a positive definition of their own.

body.text: Notice what decides the category: not what the fund buys, but how it behaves and why the regulator cares. A private credit fund and a venture capital fund can both put money into the same startup, structured as debt in one case and equity in the other, and still land in different categories, because the debt fund does not carry the same policy goal of nurturing early-stage risk capital.

children.text: Category I, II and III at a Glance
Chapters 2 to 4 dig into the sub-types and numbers inside each category. For now, hold on to the philosophy behind each one.

body.caption: The same three-factor logic, applied to each category

Pass-through: gains taxed in investors' hands, not the fund's (Chapter 5)

children.text: The philosophy behind each category also shows up in how Indian investors have actually allocated their money. According to SEBI data, total AIF commitments across all three categories stood at about ₹15.74 lakh crore as of December 2025, up close to 21% from about ₹13.05 lakh crore a year earlier.

body.title: AIF Commitments by Category, December 2025 (₹ crore)

children.text: Category II alone accounts for roughly three out of every four rupees committed to AIFs, about ₹11.64 lakh crore, because private equity and private credit are the default route for large domestic and global institutional money entering India's private markets. Category I holds the smallest share in rupee terms, about ₹97,988 crore, not because it gets less policy attention (it arguably gets the most) but because venture, angel and SME tickets are inherently smaller than a buyout or credit deal. Category III is the smallest of the three in absolute size at about ₹3.11 lakh crore, but it is growing the fastest, as more sophisticated Indian investors get comfortable with hedge-fund-style, leveraged strategies.

body.label: Category III funds raised, year on year growth
body.context: The steepest annual increase among all three AIF categories in the year to December 2025, according to SEBI data, even though Category III remains the smallest category by total commitments.

body.title: What Pulls a Fund Toward Category I vs Category III

columns.label: Pulls toward Category I
points: Funds early-stage startups, SMEs, social ventures or infrastructure
SEBI and allied policy goals want to encourage this activity
No borrowing beyond short-term operational needs
Has historically been the target of specific tax concessions (Chapter 5)

columns.label: Pulls toward Category III
points: Runs long-short, arbitrage, quant or PIPE strategies
Borrows and uses derivatives to amplify exposure
Behaves closer to a hedge fund than a long-term investor
Faces a distinct leverage ceiling and tax treatment (Chapters 4 and 5)

body.title: Which Category Does This Fund Belong To?
body.question: A fund pools ₹500 crore from HNIs and runs a long-short strategy on NSE and BSE listed stocks, using derivatives and borrowing up to the SEBI-permitted ceiling to increase its market exposure. Which category does it most likely register under?
options: It cannot register as an AIF
body.explanation: Leverage, derivatives and an active trading strategy are the exact traits that push a fund into Category III, regardless of the fact that its underlying instruments are ordinary listed shares. The category depends on how the fund behaves, not what it holds.

body.title: Classify the Chennai Distressed Debt Fund
body.scenario: A Chennai-based manager is raising ₹200 crore to buy stressed retail loans from NBFCs, restructure them, and exit over 3 to 5 years. The fund does not borrow beyond short-term working capital needs and is not targeting early-stage businesses, social ventures or infrastructure.
body.prompt: Which AIF category should this fund register under, and which of SEBI's three questions from this lesson settles it?
body.modelAnswer: Category II. It fails the first question, since buying distressed retail debt is not the kind of early-stage or socially targeted activity that earns Category I's incentive treatment. It also fails the second question, since there is no meaningful leverage or complex trading, so it is not Category III either. By elimination it lands in Category II, the residual bucket for growth and credit capital, and would get the same pass-through tax treatment and limited operational borrowing rights as a private equity fund.

cards.definition: The single regulation, effective May 2012, that replaced the narrower SEBI (Venture Capital Funds) Regulations, 1996 and created the Category I, II and III framework.
A fund investing in activity SEBI wants to encourage: venture capital, angel, SME, social venture or infrastructure. No borrowing beyond short-term operational needs.
The residual category for growth and credit capital, such as private equity, private credit, fund of funds and real estate, that is neither specially incentivised nor unusually leveraged.
A fund that trades with leverage and complexity, such as long-short, arbitrage, quant or PIPE strategies, and is regulated closer to how a hedge fund would be.
A tax treatment where the fund's gains are taxed in the hands of investors rather than the fund itself. Chapter 5 covers exactly how this applies across the three categories.

points: SEBI's three AIF categories classify behaviour and regulatory intent, not asset class.
Category I gets encouragement for funding early-stage, social or infrastructure activity that benefits the economy.
Category II is the residual bucket: growth and credit capital with no special incentive and no unusual leverage.
Category III is regulated closer to a hedge fund because it trades with leverage and complexity.
By rupee value, Category II dominates Indian AIF commitments, but Category III is growing the fastest.
The same three-factor logic (economic desirability, leverage and complexity, and the residual default) explains every sub-type covered in the next three chapters.
